questions.q: For the population $\{2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9\}$ (mean $\mu = 5$), what are the variance $\sigma^2$ and standard deviation $\sigma$ (dividing by $N$)?
questions.explain: Squared deviations: $9+1+1+1+0+0+4+16 = 32$; $\sigma^2 = 32/8 = 4$, $\sigma = \sqrt{4} = 2$. Without squaring, deviations would sum to $0$; $32$ forgets to divide by $N$.

questions.q: Heights are measured in cm. What are the units of the variance and of the standard deviation?
options: Variance in cm, standard deviation in cm²
Variance in cm², standard deviation in cm
questions.explain: Variance averages *squared* differences, so its units are squared. Taking the square root gives $\sigma$, back on the original scale — a usable "ruler" for spread.

questions.q: Why does the sample variance $s^2$ divide by $n-1$ instead of $n$?
options: To make the number bigger for safety
Because one data point is always an outlier
Measuring spread around $\bar{x}$ instead of the unknown $\mu$ biases the result downward; $n-1$ corrects that bias
Because $n-1$ makes $s$ equal to the range
questions.explain: $\bar{x}$ is fitted to the sample, so deviations around it are slightly too small on average. Dividing by $n-1$ makes $s^2$ an unbiased estimate of $\sigma^2$.

questions.q: For a normal distribution, roughly what fraction of values lies within $\mu \pm 1\sigma$?
questions.explain: $\approx 68.3\%$ lies within one standard deviation; 95.4% within $\pm 2\sigma$ and 99.7% within $\pm 3\sigma$.
